title: Present perfect vs past simple
example: I have lived here for six years. / I moved here in 2020.
explanation: Use the present perfect for a situation continuing to now; use the past simple with a finished past time reference.
question: I ___ in Boston since 2021.

title: Past perfect
example: When I arrived, the meeting had already started.
explanation: Use had + past participle for a past event preceding another past event.
question: By the time we arrived, the show ___ .

title: Mixed conditionals
example: If I had prepared earlier, I would feel calmer now.
explanation: Past unreal condition + present hypothetical result.
question: If she had saved the document, she ___ worried now.

title: Inversion for emphasis
example: Rarely have I seen such a thoughtful response.
explanation: After a negative or restrictive fronted adverbial, invert auxiliary and subject in formal English.
question: Never ___ a more convincing explanation.

title: Hedging and uncertainty
example: The result appears to suggest a possible connection.
explanation: Hedging language reduces unwarranted certainty in formal discussion.
question: Choose the cautious form: These findings ___ a link.

title: Reduced relative clauses
example: The documents submitted yesterday need review.
explanation: A passive relative clause can sometimes be shortened to a past participle phrase.
question: The report ___ last night contains corrections.

title: Cleft sentences
example: What I need is a few more minutes.
explanation: Cleft structures foreground an important part of the message.
question: ___ surprised me was her response.

title: Modal deductions
example: She must have forgotten the meeting.
explanation: Use modal + have + past participle for deductions about the past.
question: He ___ missed the train; he arrived much later than planned.

title: Passive reporting
example: The painting is believed to date from the 1800s.
explanation: Passive reporting allows cautious attribution without naming a speaker.
question: The document ___ to be authentic.

title: Emphasis with do
example: I do appreciate your help.
explanation: Use do/does/did before a base verb for emphasis.
question: I ___ understand your concern.

title: Used to vs be used to
example: I used to commute by train, but now I am used to driving.
explanation: Used to + base verb describes a past habit that no longer applies. Be used to + noun or -ing means something feels familiar now.
question: After six months, she is used to ___ early.

title: Should have vs must have
example: You should have called earlier. / She must have missed the train.
explanation: Should have + past participle expresses criticism or regret about an earlier choice. Must have + past participle is a strong deduction about a past event.
question: He is not answering. He ___ fallen asleep.

title: Would rather vs would prefer
example: I would rather stay home, but I would prefer to leave early tomorrow.
explanation: Would rather + bare infinitive; would prefer + to-infinitive. Both express preferences, with different structures.
question: We would rather ___ before rush hour.

title: Despite vs although
example: Despite the rain, we went out. / Although it was raining, we went out.
explanation: Despite / in spite of is followed by a noun or -ing clause. Although is followed by a subject and finite verb.
question: ___ being exhausted, Maya finished the report.

title: Reported questions: word order
example: She asked me where I lived. / He asked if I needed help.
explanation: Reported questions use statement word order; yes/no questions usually take if or whether. Do not preserve the original question inversion.
question: He asked me where I ___ .

title: Future perfect for deadlines
example: By Friday, we will have finished the project.
explanation: Use will have + past participle for an action expected to be complete before a specific future time.
question: By the time you arrive, I ___ dinner.

title: Causative have / get something done
example: I had my phone repaired yesterday.
explanation: Have/get + object + past participle describes arranging for another person to perform a service. The subject is not necessarily the person doing the work.
question: We are getting the roof ___ next week.

title: Hardly ... when: narrative inversion
example: Hardly had we sat down when the fire alarm rang.
explanation: When hardly appears at the start with a past-perfect sequence, invert the auxiliary and subject: Hardly had + subject + past participle + when.
question: Hardly ___ the presentation when the lights went out.

title: Not only ... but also with inversion
example: Not only did the hotel lose our booking, but it also charged us twice.
explanation: When not only introduces a clause at the beginning, invert the auxiliary and subject in the first clause. Do not invert the second clause.
question: Not only ___ the deadline, but he also forgot the attachment.

title: Wish + past perfect for regret
example: I wish I had checked the address before leaving.
explanation: Wish + had + past participle expresses regret about something that happened or failed to happen in the past. Wish + past simple instead expresses a present unreal situation.
question: I wish we ___ the earlier flight yesterday.
